title: Fibers and Fabrics
bigQuestion: Why do two shirts that look alike on the hanger behave so differently once you wear, wash and wear them again?

story.title: The Shirt That Dried First
story.kicker: A rainstorm on the walk home turns into a fiber lesson that Dev did not plan on learning.
paragraphs: The rain started three blocks from Dev's building and did not let up. By the time he got inside, his gym shirt, his jeans and his cotton hoodie were soaked through. He peeled everything off, hung it all over the shower rod, and went to do homework. Two hours later he came back to change. The gym shirt was dry enough to wear. The hoodie was damp and heavy. The jeans were still wet at the seams and would be until morning.

It bothered him. Same rain, same shower rod, same two hours. He pulled the tag out of the gym shirt collar: 100% polyester. The hoodie tag said 80% cotton, 20% polyester. The jeans said 99% cotton, 1% spandex. He had read those tags a hundred times without reading them. Now they looked like the answer to a question he had just asked.

In class the next day Ms. Reyes had a tray of fabric squares on every table. She asked the class to drop one drop of water on each square and count how long it took to soak in. On the cotton the drop vanished in two seconds. On the polyester the drop sat up like a bead for almost a minute. "Cotton pulls water in and holds it," she said. "That is why your towel is cotton. Polyester does not. That is why your gym shirt is polyester."

Dev thought about the jeans. Cotton, and thick, and woven tight. Of course they held water. He thought about his hoodie, fleecy and mostly cotton. Ms. Reyes was already writing on the board: fiber, then yarn, then fabric, then finish. "Everything a piece of clothing does starts with the fiber," she said. "Warm or cool, stretchy or stiff, quick to dry or slow, wrinkled or smooth. Learn the fibers and you can read any shirt before you buy it."

That afternoon Dev went through his drawer and read every tag. He sorted the pile without meaning to: the things he wore to run, the things he wore when it was cold, the things that came out of the dryer wrinkled. Every pile had a fiber in common. It was the first time his closet had ever made sense.
story.think: Dev read his clothing tags for years without noticing them. What is one piece of clothing you own that behaves in a way a fiber could explain?

lessons.title: Cotton and Linen
lessons.mainIdea: Cotton and linen are plant fibers that absorb water, breathe well and wrinkle easily, which makes them comfortable in heat and slow to dry.
reading: Pull a cotton T-shirt out of the dryer and it is warm, soft and a little wrinkled. Pull a polyester shirt out and it is smooth. The difference starts inside the fiber. A *fiber* is the smallest hair-like unit that fabric is made from. Cotton grows as a fluff around the seeds of the cotton plant, and each fiber is a hollow tube of *cellulose*, the material plant walls are built from. That tube soaks up water like a tiny straw, which is why cotton feels cool in summer and why a cotton towel dries you off.

Cotton is strong, gets a little stronger when wet, and stands up to hot water and repeated washing. It takes dye well, which is why so much printed fabric is cotton. Its weaknesses are the other side of the same coin. Because it holds water it dries slowly, and because the fibers do not spring back, it wrinkles and can shrink in a hot dryer. Cotton is the fiber in T-shirts, jeans, sheets, towels and most underwear.

*Linen* comes from the stem of the flax plant. Workers soak the stems to loosen the fibers, then comb them out into long, stiff strands. Linen is also cellulose, so it absorbs and breathes like cotton, but the fibers are longer and stiffer. Linen is one of the strongest natural fibers and feels crisp and cool. It also wrinkles more than any other common fabric. A linen shirt looks creased ten minutes after you iron it, and people who wear linen learn to accept that.

A common mistake is to treat cotton like it cannot shrink. A new pair of 100% cotton pants washed in hot water and dried on high can lose an inch in length the first time. If the label says cold wash and low heat, that is why. Another mistake is buying a cotton shirt to run in on a hot day. It will soak up sweat, hold it against your skin, and get heavy. For that job a fiber that does not absorb is the better choice, which the next lessons explain.

words.d: the smallest hair-like strand that yarn and fabric are made from
the material plant cell walls are made of; cotton, linen and rayon are cellulose fibers
a strong, crisp, cool fiber made from the stem of the flax plant
able to soak up and hold water

look.title: One Drop of Water
look.text: Four fabric squares lie on a table: a cotton bandana, a linen napkin, a polyester gym shirt scrap and a wool sock cuff. You put one drop of water on each. On the bandana the drop disappears in about two seconds. On the napkin it soaks in almost as fast. On the polyester the drop sits like a bead for close to a minute. On the wool it sits for a while, then slowly sinks in.
look.prompt: Which two squares are cellulose fibers, and how did the water tell you? Which square would you want as a towel, and which as a rain jacket lining?

check.q: Why does a cotton towel dry you off well?
choices: Cotton fibers are hollow tubes of cellulose that soak up water
Cotton fibers repel water so it rolls off your skin
Cotton is a protein fiber that warms the water
Cotton fibers melt slightly and grip the water
check.why: Cotton fibers are hollow cellulose tubes that pull water in and hold it, which makes cotton highly absorbent.

check.q: A new pair of 100% cotton pants came out of a hot wash and a high-heat dryer an inch shorter. What happened?
choices: The dye tightened the fabric
Cotton shrinks in hot water and high dryer heat
The pants were mislabeled polyester
Cotton stretches when wet and then snaps back too far
check.why: Cotton can shrink in hot water and high heat, which is why many cotton labels call for cold wash and low or medium dryer heat.

check.q: Which plant does linen come from?
choices: The cotton plant
The bamboo plant
The flax plant
The hemp plant
check.why: Linen is spun from long fibers taken out of the stem of the flax plant.

lessons.title: Wool and Silk
lessons.mainIdea: Wool and silk are protein fibers from animals; wool traps warm air and resists wrinkles, while silk is smooth, strong and delicate to care for.
reading: Put your hand inside a wool sweater on a cold morning and it feels warm before you have even worn it. *Wool* is the fleece of sheep, sheared off once a year and spun into yarn. Each wool fiber is a *protein* fiber, like your own hair, and it grows with a natural wave called crimp. When wool is spun, those crimped fibers trap millions of tiny pockets of air. Trapped air is what keeps you warm, so wool insulates even when it is a little damp.

Wool has two more useful habits. The crimp acts like a spring, so wool springs back from folds and does not wrinkle much. And the surface of each fiber is covered in tiny overlapping scales, like shingles on a roof. Those scales are also its weak point. Hot water plus rubbing makes the scales lock together, the fibers pull tight, and the sweater felts into something two sizes smaller. That is why wool labels say hand wash cold or dry clean, and lay flat to dry.

*Silk* is spun by the silkworm caterpillar as it builds its cocoon. The cocoon is one continuous thread up to a few thousand feet long, unwound by workers in warm water. Silk is a protein fiber like wool, but smooth instead of scaly, which gives it a soft shine and a cool, slippery feel. For its weight it is very strong. It is also easily damaged: sunlight fades it, sweat and deodorant stain it, and a hot iron scorches it.

The common mistake with both fibers is washing them like cotton. A wool sweater thrown in a hot wash and a hot dryer will come out felted and small, and nothing will stretch it back. A silk blouse in the same load will lose its shine and may shrink or bleed dye. Read the tag, wash in cold water by hand or on a gentle cycle, and lay wool flat to dry so its own wet weight does not stretch it out of shape.

words.d: the fleece of sheep, a crimped protein fiber that traps air and keeps you warm
a fiber from an animal, such as wool or silk; hair is a protein fiber too
the smooth, strong, shiny fiber a silkworm spins to build its cocoon
wool fibers locking together and shrinking when hot water and rubbing make their scales catch

look.title: The Sweater in the Dryer
look.text: Aaron's older sister gave him a gray wool sweater that fit perfectly. He wore it for a week, then washed it with his jeans on the hot cycle and dried it on high. It came out stiff, dense and small enough for his eight-year-old cousin. The tag, which he reads now, says: hand wash cold, lay flat to dry, or dry clean.
look.prompt: Name the two things in the wash that made the sweater felt. Could anything bring it back to size? What should Aaron do with the next wool sweater?

check.q: Why does wool keep you warm even when it is a little damp?
choices: Wool fibers give off heat as they dry
Wool fibers absorb no water at all
Wool is thicker than any other fiber
Crimped wool fibers trap pockets of air that hold in body heat
check.why: Wool's natural crimp traps air between fibers, and trapped air insulates, even when the fibers hold some moisture.

check.q: A wool sweater washed hot and dried on high comes out two sizes smaller. What happened to the fibers?
choices: The scales on the fibers locked together and felted
The fibers dissolved partly in the hot water
The dye shrank the yarn
The fibers melted and hardened
check.why: Heat and rubbing make the overlapping scales on wool fibers catch and lock, pulling the fabric tight; this felting cannot be undone.

check.q: What do wool and silk have in common?
choices: Both come from plants
Both are protein fibers from animals
Both are made in a factory from oil
Both are scaly on the surface
check.why: Wool comes from sheep and silk from silkworms; both are protein fibers, though silk is smooth and wool is scaly.

lessons.title: Polyester and Nylon
lessons.mainIdea: Polyester and nylon are made from petroleum; they dry fast, resist wrinkles and hold their shape, but they melt under high heat and do not breathe like plant fibers.
reading: The gym shirt that dried in two hours was polyester. *Polyester* is a *manufactured fiber*, which means it does not grow on a plant or an animal; it is made in a factory. Chemists start with petroleum, build long chain molecules from it, melt the plastic, and force it through a metal plate with tiny holes called a spinneret. Each hole makes one continuous fiber, like a strand of very fine fishing line. Because the fiber is solid plastic, water cannot get inside it. It dries fast, does not shrink, and springs back from wrinkles.

Those habits make polyester the most used fiber in the world. It goes into athletic wear, fleece jackets, school uniforms, curtains and the thread in most sewing kits. Its weaknesses come from the same plastic nature. It does not absorb sweat, so on a hot day a polyester shirt can feel clammy unless it is knit with channels that move moisture. It holds onto body odor more than cotton. And it melts: an iron on the cotton setting will glaze or put a hole in polyester in seconds. Always iron it on low or not at all.

*Nylon* was the first fully manufactured fiber, made in the 1930s, and it is even stronger than polyester. It stretches a little and snaps back, resists scrapes, and dries fast. That is why nylon is in backpacks, tents, windbreakers, swimsuits, stockings and seat belts. Like polyester it melts with heat and does not breathe. It also weakens in strong sunlight over years, so an old nylon tent can tear where a new one would not.

A common mistake is thinking a fast-drying shirt is always cooler. On a humid day, a polyester shirt without moisture-wicking channels can feel hotter than cotton because sweat sits between skin and fabric. Another is putting polyester fleece in a hot dryer; it does not shrink, but it pills, meaning small balls of fiber form on the surface. Low heat, or a line, keeps it looking new longer.

words.d: a fiber made in a factory rather than grown; polyester, nylon, rayon and spandex are examples
a strong plastic fiber made from petroleum that dries fast, resists wrinkles and melts under high heat
the first fully manufactured fiber; very strong, slightly stretchy and quick to dry
small balls of tangled fiber that form on a fabric's surface from rubbing

look.title: An Iron on the Wrong Setting
look.text: Priya is pressing a pile of clothes before a family event. She sets the iron to the cotton setting, presses two cotton shirts, and then slides the iron onto her brother's black polyester dress shirt. The fabric under the iron goes shiny and stiff, and a faint smell rises. When she lifts the iron, a glossy iron-shaped patch is left on the back of the shirt.
look.prompt: What happened to the polyester fibers under the iron? What setting should Priya have used, and what should she check on every garment before she presses it?

check.q: Why does a polyester shirt dry so much faster than a cotton one?
choices: Polyester fibers are thinner than cotton fibers
Polyester is always knit, and knits dry fast
Polyester fibers are solid plastic that water cannot soak into
Polyester fibers give off heat that evaporates water
check.why: Polyester is a solid plastic fiber; water stays on the surface instead of soaking in, so it evaporates quickly.

check.q: An iron on the cotton setting leaves a shiny, stiff patch on a polyester shirt. What happened?
choices: The shirt shrank under the iron
The dye burned off the fabric
The fibers absorbed steam and swelled
The plastic fibers melted and glazed
check.why: Polyester is a plastic that melts at ironing temperatures meant for cotton; it must be pressed on low or not at all.

check.q: Which fiber is most likely in a backpack, a tent and a seat belt?
choices: Nylon, because it is very strong and resists scrapes
Linen, because it is the strongest natural fiber
Wool, because it springs back from folds
Rayon, because it drapes well
check.why: Nylon's strength, slight stretch and scrape resistance make it the standard fiber for gear that takes hard wear.

lessons.title: Rayon and Spandex
lessons.mainIdea: Rayon is made from wood pulp and drapes like silk but is weak when wet; spandex stretches several times its length and returns, so a little of it changes how a garment fits.
reading: Not every manufactured fiber starts as oil. *Rayon* starts as wood pulp or cotton scraps, which are cellulose, the same material as cotton. The pulp is dissolved in chemicals into a thick liquid, then pushed through a spinneret into a bath that hardens it back into fiber. The result is a plant-based fiber that a factory shaped. Rayon is soft, absorbent, cool and drapes in smooth folds like silk, at a fraction of the cost. You will see it on the tags of dresses, blouses and linings, sometimes under the name viscose.

Rayon's weakness is water. It absorbs like cotton, but unlike cotton it gets much weaker when wet. A rayon dress agitated in a washing machine can stretch, twist, shrink or tear at the seams while it is soaked, and a hot dryer can shrink it further. Many rayon labels say dry clean only or hand wash cold and lay flat, and those instructions are not a suggestion. Treat wet rayon gently, support its weight, and let it dry before you pull on it.

*Spandex* is the fiber that makes clothes stretch. It is a manufactured fiber built from long chain molecules that can extend to several times their length and snap back. On its own it is never used; it is blended in small amounts, often 2 to 10 percent, with cotton, polyester or nylon. Dev's jeans with 1% spandex bend at the knee more easily than stiff denim. Leggings, swimsuits and athletic wear carry more. You may see it called elastane or by a brand name.

The common mistake with spandex is heat. High dryer heat and hot irons damage the stretchy molecules, and over time the fabric bags out and stops recovering. Chlorine from pools does the same to a swimsuit, which is why rinsing a suit in cool water after swimming makes it last. Wash stretch garments cool and dry them low or hang them, and they will keep their snap for years.

words.d: a manufactured cellulose fiber made from wood pulp; soft and drapey but weak when wet
a manufactured fiber that stretches several times its length and returns; also called elastane
the way a fabric hangs and falls in folds
a yarn or fabric made of two or more fibers mixed together, such as 95% cotton, 5% spandex

look.title: Spandex on the Tag
look.cite: Example fiber-content tags; actual percentages vary by garment
look.prompt: Why does a pair of jeans need so much less spandex than a swimsuit? What would happen to each garment if the spandex lost its snap?

check.q: Rayon is made in a factory, yet it is a cellulose fiber. Why?
choices: It is a plastic made to imitate cotton
It starts as wood pulp, which is plant cellulose, and is reshaped into fiber
It is spun from silkworm cocoons in a factory
It is cotton that has been bleached and softened
check.why: Rayon is regenerated cellulose: wood pulp dissolved and forced through a spinneret, so its raw material is plant cellulose.

check.q: A rayon dress twisted and tore at a seam in a normal wash cycle. What property of rayon explains it?
choices: Rayon melts in warm water
Rayon felts when rubbed
Rayon loses much of its strength when wet
Rayon stretches like spandex and snapped
check.why: Rayon is much weaker wet than dry, so a soaked dress agitated in a machine can stretch, twist or tear.

check.q: Why is spandex almost never used by itself?
choices: It is blended in small amounts to give other fibers stretch and recovery
It absorbs too much water to wear alone
It is too warm for any garment
It cannot be dyed
check.why: A few percent of spandex blended with cotton, polyester or nylon gives a garment stretch and recovery; alone it has no body.

lessons.title: Reading the Fiber Tag
lessons.mainIdea: U.S. law requires most clothing to carry a tag listing every fiber by percentage, and reading it tells you how the garment will feel, wear and wash before you buy.
reading: Look inside the collar or side seam of almost any garment sold in the United States and you will find a small tag. Federal law, the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act, requires it to list each *fiber content* by percentage in order from most to least, the country where the garment was made, and the name or registered number of the company responsible. A separate federal rule requires care instructions on the same tag or a nearby one. Those few lines are the most honest thing about the garment.

Read the percentages as a recipe. "100% cotton" will breathe, absorb, wrinkle and possibly shrink. "60% cotton, 40% polyester" will breathe less but wrinkle less and dry faster, and it will hold up in a hot dryer better than pure cotton. "95% rayon, 5% spandex" will drape and stretch and needs gentle washing. "100% wool" needs cold water and flat drying. Once you know the fibers, every tag predicts the future of the garment.

A *blend* takes the strengths of two fibers and softens the weaknesses of each. Cotton-polyester sheets breathe almost like cotton and come out of the dryer nearly smooth. Wool-nylon socks feel warm like wool and wear at the heel like nylon. But a blend also takes both fibers' care rules. A 50/50 shirt should be ironed on the polyester setting, not the cotton one, because the polyester half will still melt.

The mistake shoppers make is judging by feel on the rack. A soft, smooth shirt might be rayon that will fall apart in the wash, or polyester that will feel clammy in July. A stiff cotton shirt will soften with washing. Take ten seconds and turn the tag out. If a tag is missing entirely on a new garment, that is a sign about the seller too.

words.d: the list of fibers in a fabric by percentage, required on clothing tags by U.S. law
the tag that gives washing, drying, bleaching and ironing instructions for a garment
the U.S. law that requires fiber content, country of origin and maker identification on textile products

look.title: Three Tags, One Shelf
look.text: Three black T-shirts hang side by side at the same price. Tag one: 100% cotton, machine wash warm, tumble dry medium. Tag two: 50% cotton, 50% polyester, machine wash warm, tumble dry low. Tag three: 95% rayon, 5% spandex, hand wash cold, lay flat to dry. Your cousin wants a shirt for summer camp where laundry is a hot machine wash and a hot dryer once a week.
look.prompt: Which shirt should your cousin take to camp and why? What is likely to happen to each of the other two after a summer of camp laundry?

check.q: On a U.S. clothing tag, fibers are listed in what order?
choices: Alphabetical order
Natural fibers first, then manufactured
Most expensive fiber first
Highest percentage first, down to the lowest
check.why: Federal law requires fiber content by percentage in descending order, largest share first.

check.q: A tag reads 50% cotton, 50% polyester. Which iron setting is safe?
choices: The cotton setting, since it is half cotton
The polyester (low) setting, because the polyester half can still melt
The hottest setting, to smooth both fibers
No setting; blends cannot be ironed
check.why: A blend takes the care limits of its most delicate fiber; polyester melts at cotton-setting heat, so press on low.

check.q: Why does a 60% cotton, 40% polyester shirt come out of the dryer smoother than a 100% cotton shirt?
choices: Polyester weighs more and pulls the wrinkles out
Cotton shrinks around the polyester
Polyester fibers spring back from wrinkles and hold the blend flat
The blend absorbs more water and dries slower
check.why: Polyester resists wrinkles, so its share in a blend keeps the fabric smoother than pure cotton.

lessons.title: Woven or Knit
lessons.mainIdea: Woven fabric is made of yarns crossing at right angles and barely stretches; knit fabric is made of loops and stretches, which decides how each is sewn, worn and washed.
reading: Pull the hem of a T-shirt sideways and it stretches; pull the hem of a dress shirt and it does not. Both are cotton, so the fiber is not the reason. The difference is how the yarn became fabric. First, fibers are twisted together into *yarn*, a continuous strand strong enough to work with. Then yarn becomes cloth in one of two main ways: woven or knit. The construction changes how the fabric stretches, frays, wrinkles and hangs more than most people realize.

*Woven* fabric is made on a loom. Long yarns run the length of the cloth; a second yarn passes over and under them, back and forth, across the width. The yarns cross at right angles like a tiny grid. Because the yarns are straight and locked, a woven barely stretches along its length or width, holds a crisp shape, and can be pressed into sharp creases. Cut a woven and the edge frays as loose yarns slip out. Jeans, dress shirts, sheets, jackets and most pants are woven.

*Knit* fabric is made of one or more yarns looped through each other row by row, the way a hand-knitted scarf is, only with far finer loops. Each loop can open and close, so knits stretch in every direction and spring back. That is why a T-shirt pulls over your head without buttons and why leggings fit. Knits do not wrinkle much, drape softly, and do not fray, though a cut edge can curl and a broken loop can run into a ladder. T-shirts, sweatshirts, socks, underwear and sweaters are knits.

The common mistake is sewing or fitting a knit like a woven. A knit needs a stitch that stretches with it, such as a zigzag, or the seam pops the first time you pull the shirt on. A woven pattern needs extra room, called ease, because the fabric will not give. And a heavy knit sweater hung on a hanger will stretch under its own weight at the shoulders, so knits are folded and wovens are hung.

words.d: a continuous strand made by twisting fibers together; fabric is made from yarn
fabric made of yarns crossing at right angles on a loom; crisp, stable and prone to fraying
fabric made of yarn looped through itself row by row; stretchy and resistant to wrinkles
loose yarns coming out of a cut edge of woven fabric

look.title: Sort the Laundry Basket
look.text: A laundry basket holds a pair of jeans, a cotton T-shirt, a button-front flannel shirt, a pair of socks, a hooded sweatshirt, a pillowcase, a pair of leggings and a wool sweater. You have to sort them into two piles: things to hang and things to fold. The rule from the lesson is that knits stretch under their own weight and wovens do not.
look.prompt: Put each item in the woven pile or the knit pile, then say which pile gets hangers. How can you tell a knit from a woven with your hands if the tag is gone?

check.q: Why does a T-shirt stretch when you pull it and a dress shirt does not, even when both are cotton?
choices: The T-shirt is knit from loops that open; the dress shirt is woven from straight crossing yarns
The T-shirt has more cotton in it
The dress shirt is starched at the factory
The T-shirt is thinner, so it gives more
check.why: Construction, not fiber, sets the stretch: knit loops open and close, while woven yarns are straight and locked.

check.q: A student sews a knit T-shirt seam with a plain straight stitch. What happens when she pulls it on?
choices: The seam stretches and stays fine
The fabric frays away from the seam
The seam shrinks in the wash
The thread pops because the straight stitch cannot stretch with the knit
check.why: Knits stretch and a straight stitch does not, so the thread breaks; knits need a zigzag or other stretch stitch.

check.q: Which fabric problem happens to wovens but not to knits?
choices: Curling at a cut edge
Fraying at a cut edge
A run or ladder from a broken loop
Stretching out on a hanger
check.why: Cut woven edges fray as loose yarns slip out; knit edges curl or run instead.

lessons.title: Plain, Twill and Satin
lessons.mainIdea: The three basic weaves, plain, twill and satin, change how a woven fabric looks, wears and drapes: plain is even and crisp, twill is diagonal and tough, satin is smooth and shiny.
reading: Lay a bandana, a pair of jeans and a shiny ribbon side by side. All three are woven, but they look nothing alike. The reason is the *weave*, the pattern in which the crosswise yarn passes over and under the lengthwise yarns. Three patterns cover most of what you wear. Learn them and you can name a fabric from across the room.

In a *plain weave* the crosswise yarn goes over one, under one, over one, under one, and the next row shifts by one. It is the simplest and most common weave. The surface looks the same on both sides, it is strong for its weight, and it wrinkles readily. Bandanas, muslin, broadcloth shirts, quilting cotton, chiffon and most bedsheets are plain weaves.

In a *twill weave* the yarn goes over two or three and under one, and each row shifts by one, so the crossing points step across the fabric in a diagonal line. Look closely at jeans and you will see those diagonal ridges. Twill packs yarns tighter, so it is heavier, tougher, resists dirt and wrinkles less than plain weave. Denim, chinos, gabardine and most work pants are twills.

In a *satin weave* one yarn floats over four or more yarns before dipping under one. Those long floats lie flat and reflect light, which gives satin its shine and its slippery feel. The floats also snag easily and wear faster, which is why satin is for dresses, linings and ribbons, not for work pants. The common mistake is calling satin a fiber. It is a weave; satin can be silk, polyester or cotton, and the tag tells you which.

words.d: the pattern in which crosswise yarns pass over and under lengthwise yarns in a woven fabric
over one, under one; the simplest and most common weave, as in bandanas and sheets
a weave with a diagonal line on the surface, as in denim and chinos; tough and dirt-hiding
a weave with long floating yarns that make a smooth, shiny, snag-prone surface

look.title: How Far a Yarn Floats
look.cite: Standard weave structures; satin floats can be longer than four
look.prompt: As the float gets longer, what happens to the fabric's shine and to its risk of snagging? Which weave would you pick for work pants, and which for a ribbon?

check.q: You see fine diagonal ridges running across a pair of pants. What weave is it?
choices: Plain weave
Satin weave
Twill weave
Knit
check.why: The stepping over-under pattern of twill produces a visible diagonal line, as in denim and chinos.

check.q: Why is satin shiny?
choices: It is always made of silk
Long yarn floats lie flat on the surface and reflect light
The yarns are coated with plastic
It is pressed with a very hot iron at the factory
check.why: In a satin weave a yarn floats over four or more yarns; the flat floats reflect light, whatever the fiber.

check.q: A tag says 100% polyester satin. What does the word satin tell you?
choices: The fiber is silk, not polyester
The fabric is knit
The fabric was dyed shiny
The weave has long floats, so it will be smooth but snag easily
check.why: Satin names a weave, not a fiber; the polyester tells you the fiber and the satin tells you the structure.

lessons.title: Choosing by Property
lessons.mainIdea: Every fabric trades off breathability, stretch, warmth and durability, and the right choice matches those properties to the job the garment has to do.
reading: Ms. Reyes gives the class a job: pick a fabric for a soccer jersey, a winter coat lining and a pair of work pants for a summer landscaping job. Nobody can answer with a fiber alone. You have to weigh four *properties*, the ways a fabric behaves: breathability, stretch, warmth and durability. Each is set by fiber, yarn and construction together, and no fabric wins on all four.

*Breathability* is how easily air and moisture pass through. Loosely woven or knit plant fibers breathe best; tightly woven manufactured fibers breathe least, unless they are knit with wicking channels. Stretch comes mostly from construction and spandex: a knit stretches, a woven does not, and a few percent of spandex makes either one give. Warmth comes from trapped air, so fuzzy, crimped or thick fabrics such as wool, fleece and flannel are warm even when they are light.

*Durability* is resistance to wear, tearing and repeated washing. Nylon, polyester and tight twills such as denim are the toughest. Satin, loose knits, rayon and silk wear fastest. So the soccer jersey wants breathability and stretch: a polyester knit with wicking. The coat lining wants warmth and low friction: fleece or a smooth quilted lining. The work pants want durability and some breathability: cotton twill, maybe with 2% spandex for bending.

The common mistake is choosing on one property and forgetting the others. A heavy wool coat is warm and tough, but it soaks up rain and takes a day to dry. A thin polyester shirt is quick-drying and durable, but on a still, humid day it can feel like a plastic bag. When you shop or sew, say out loud what the garment has to do, list the two properties that matter most, and pick the fabric that serves those.

words.d: a way a fabric behaves, such as how much it stretches, breathes, warms or wears
how easily air and moisture pass through a fabric
how well a fabric stands up to wear, tearing and repeated washing
a knit built with channels that pull sweat away from the skin to the surface to evaporate

look.title: Three Jobs, Three Fabrics
look.text: Fabric options on the table: cotton plain-weave broadcloth; polyester wicking knit; cotton twill with 2% spandex; wool flannel; polyester fleece; rayon challis; nylon ripstop. Jobs to fill: a jersey for a July soccer tournament, the lining of a winter coat, and pants for a summer job hauling mulch and bending all day.
look.prompt: Match a fabric to each job and name the two properties that decided it. Which fabric on the table would be wrong for all three jobs, and why?

check.q: Which two properties matter most for a summer soccer jersey?
choices: Breathability and stretch
Warmth and durability
Shine and drape
Warmth and stretch
check.why: A jersey for hot play needs to move with the body and let sweat out, which points to a wicking polyester knit.

check.q: What gives fleece and flannel their warmth?
choices: Their fibers give off heat
Their yarns are made of wool
Their fuzzy surface traps pockets of air
They are woven very tightly
check.why: Warmth comes from trapped air, and a fuzzy or crimped surface holds many small air pockets.

check.q: A student chooses a heavy wool coat for a rainy fall walk to school. What property did he forget?
choices: Wool is not warm enough
Wool has too much stretch
Wool is not durable
Wool absorbs rain and dries slowly
check.why: Wool is warm and tough, but it soaks up water and takes a long time to dry, a poor match for steady rain.

lessons.title: Care Label Symbols
lessons.mainIdea: Five care symbols, washtub, triangle, square, iron and circle, plus dots for heat and an X for never, tell you how to wash any garment without a single word.
reading: A sweater tag shows a tub of water with one dot, a triangle with an X through it, a square with three lines inside, an iron with one dot, and a circle. No words. Those five symbols are the standard *care symbols* used on U.S. clothing since the late 1990s, and once you know them you can read the tag on anything. Each symbol is one step of laundry, and the marks inside it say how.

The *washtub* means washing. Dots inside it give the water temperature: one dot cold, two dots warm, three dots hot. A hand in the tub means hand wash. An X over the tub means do not wash; dry clean instead. The *triangle* means bleach: plain means any bleach is safe, diagonal lines inside mean only non-chlorine bleach, an X means no bleach. Chlorine bleach on a triangle-with-X garment can strip color or eat holes in the fiber.

The square means drying. A circle inside the square means tumble dry, with dots for heat: one dot low, two medium, three high, and an X for no tumble drying. Lines inside the square without a circle mean air drying: a curved line at the top means hang to dry, one horizontal line means lay flat. The iron symbol takes the same dots, one for low, two for medium, three for high, and an X means do not iron. A circle alone means dry clean; a circle with an X means do not dry clean.

So the sweater tag reads: wash cold, no bleach, lay flat to dry, iron on low, dry clean is fine. The common mistake is skipping the tag and washing everything one way. That is how wool felts, rayon tears, polyester glazes and a bright red shirt turns a load of whites pink. Read the five symbols the first time you own a garment. After that you will remember.

words.d: the standard picture symbols on clothing tags that show how to wash, bleach, dry, iron and dry clean
the tub-of-water picture that means washing; dots give the water temperature
marks inside a care symbol that set the heat: one dot low or cold, two medium or warm, three high or hot
color-safe oxygen bleach; shown by a triangle with diagonal lines inside

look.title: Dots and Heat
look.cite: ASTM D5489 care symbols as used on U.S. garment labels
look.prompt: A tag shows a washtub with one dot and a dryer square with an X. Say the instruction in words. What would happen to a wool sweater washed at three dots?

check.q: A care tag shows a triangle with an X through it. What does it mean?
choices: Do not iron
Do not bleach
Do not tumble dry
Do not dry clean
check.why: The triangle stands for bleach; an X through it means no bleach of any kind.

check.q: Which symbol means lay flat to dry?
choices: A square with a circle inside
A circle with an X
A square with one horizontal line inside
A washtub with a hand
check.why: The square is drying; a single horizontal line inside, with no circle, means dry flat.

check.q: A washtub symbol has three dots. What temperature should you use?
choices: Cold
Warm
Rinse only
Hot
check.why: Dots count up with heat: one is cold, two is warm and three is hot.

lessons.title: The Burn Test, Described
lessons.mainIdea: Textile labs identify an unknown fiber by how a snip of it burns; you will read the results here, not perform them, because open flame near fabric is a fire hazard.
reading: When a tag is missing, a textile lab can name the fiber with a *burn test*: a technician holds a tiny snip of fabric in tweezers over a metal tray and touches it to a flame. This lesson describes what they see. It is not a lesson to try at home or in class. Loose fabric catches instantly, melting plastic drips and sticks to skin, and the fumes from some fibers are toxic. You will identify fibers by tag, feel and water drop instead.

The lab watches three things: how the sample acts near the flame, how it burns, and what is left. Cotton, linen and rayon, the cellulose fibers, catch fast, burn with a yellow flame, keep burning after the flame is removed, smell like burning paper, and leave a soft, light gray ash that crumbles. Wool and silk, the protein fibers, catch slowly, sputter, tend to go out on their own when the flame is pulled away, smell like burning hair, and leave a crisp black bead that crushes to powder.

Polyester and nylon behave like the plastics they are. They shrink and curl away from the flame before touching it, melt as they burn, drip, smell chemical or sweet, and leave a hard round bead that does not crush. Spandex melts into a sticky black bead. Blends show a mix: a cotton-polyester sample smells of paper and leaves a hard bead with ash around it. These are the standard lab results and the reason a chemist can read a fabric no tag describes.

The lesson for you is the hazard, not the test. Fabrics burn in the kitchen the same way they burn under tweezers. A loose cotton sleeve over a gas burner catches and keeps burning. A polyester fleece near a flame melts onto skin, which is a far worse burn than a scorch. Wool is the slowest to catch and tends to put itself out, which is why firefighters and welders wear it. Keep sleeves rolled and fabric away from flames, and choose fibers with fire in mind.

words.d: a lab method of naming a fiber by how a tiny sample acts in a flame; not for home or classroom use
the soft gray powder left when a cellulose fiber such as cotton burns
the hard lump left when a plastic fiber such as polyester melts and cools
going out on its own once the flame is removed, as wool tends to do

look.title: Fiber Groups and Flame
rows: cellulose fibers: keep burning after flame removed (yes=1)
protein fibers: keep burning after flame removed
plastic fibers: keep burning after flame removed
look.cite: Standard textile burn-test descriptions used in fiber identification
look.prompt: Which fiber group is safest to wear near a stove, according to these rows? Which group is most dangerous when it burns, and why is melting worse than charring?

check.q: Why is the burn test described in this course but never performed?
choices: The results are not reliable
It only works on natural fibers
Fabric catches instantly and melting plastic sticks to skin
It requires expensive equipment
check.why: Open flame near fabric is a serious burn and fire hazard; students identify fibers by tag, feel and water instead.

check.q: A lab sample melts, drips and leaves a hard bead that will not crush. What kind of fiber is it?
choices: Cotton or linen
Wool or silk
Rayon
Polyester or nylon
check.why: Plastic fibers melt and cool into a hard bead; cellulose leaves ash and protein leaves a crushable black bead.

check.q: Why do firefighters and welders often wear wool?
choices: Wool catches slowly and tends to go out on its own
Wool never gets hot
Wool melts into a protective layer
Wool is the cheapest fiber
check.why: Protein fibers like wool are slow to catch and self-extinguishing, unlike cotton, which keeps burning, or polyester, which melts.

lessons.title: Fast Fashion and Its Cost
lessons.mainIdea: Cheap, quickly made clothing costs water, energy and labor to produce and mostly ends up in landfills, so buying less, choosing durable fibers and caring for clothes is a real choice with real effects.
reading: A five-dollar T-shirt is on a rack in a mall on the far edge of Chicago. It is cheaper than a sandwich. That price is possible because of *fast fashion*: designing, making and shipping new styles in weeks, in huge numbers, from the lowest-cost fabric and labor, so a shirt can be worn a few times and replaced. The price on the tag does not include everything the shirt cost.

Some of that cost is water and energy. Growing cotton takes large amounts of water; making polyester takes petroleum and energy, and washing polyester sheds tiny plastic fibers into water systems. Some of the cost is people. Most cheap clothing is sewn in factories far away, and garment workers in some of those factories work long hours for low pay in unsafe buildings. Some of the cost lands at the end. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency estimated that in 2018 Americans sent about 11 million tons of textiles to landfills.

None of this means new clothes are wrong. It means the choices you already learned in this chapter have weight. A durable fabric, cotton twill instead of a loose knit, lasts more washes. A garment you can mend stays out of the trash. A tag you read keeps a sweater from felting after one wash. *Secondhand* clothing, from thrift stores and swaps, gives a garment a second life at a fraction of the cost. And a cold wash and a line dry use less energy than hot and high.

The common mistake is to think the answer is a better brand. The most effective change is fewer, better, longer. Buy what you will wear thirty times. Learn what the fibers do so the garment matches the job. Wash it as the label says. Fix it when it tears. A closet built that way costs less over a year than a closet of five-dollar shirts, and it puts far less in the ground.

words.d: clothing designed, made and sold quickly and cheaply in large volumes, meant to be replaced often
previously owned clothing sold or passed on, as in a thrift store or a clothing swap
clothing and fabric thrown away instead of reused, mended or recycled
built to last through many wears and washes

look.title: Cost per Wear (Example)
look.cite: Example figures: price divided by number of times worn
look.prompt: Which shirt is the cheapest per wear? What has to be true about the $20 shirt for it to beat the $5 one, and which fabric choices from this chapter make that more likely?

check.q: What does cost per wear measure?
choices: The price of a garment plus its washing cost
The price of a garment divided by the number of times it is worn
The price of a garment compared to a brand-name one
How much a garment costs to make
check.why: Cost per wear is price divided by wears; a $20 shirt worn 100 times costs $0.20 per wear.

check.q: Which choice does the most to reduce textile waste?
choices: Buying the newest styles as soon as they come out
Washing everything hot so it is very clean
Buying fewer, more durable garments and mending them
Choosing only manufactured fibers
check.why: Fewer, longer-lasting, mended garments stay out of landfills; hot washing and constant replacement do the opposite.

check.q: Why does washing polyester have an environmental effect beyond energy use?
choices: It uses more water than cotton
It releases dye into rivers
It felts and clogs machines
It sheds tiny plastic fibers into the water
check.why: Polyester is plastic, and washing sheds microfibers into wastewater; cold, less frequent washing reduces it.

review.q: Which fiber is a protein fiber?
choices: Cotton
Rayon
Wool
Polyester
review.why: Wool and silk come from animals and are protein fibers; cotton and rayon are cellulose and polyester is plastic.

review.q: A shirt tag reads 100% linen. What should you expect?
choices: Cool, crisp, strong and quick to wrinkle
Stretchy and quick to dry
Warm and prone to felting
Shiny and slippery
review.why: Linen, from flax, is a strong cool cellulose fiber that wrinkles more than any other common fabric.

review.q: Rayon and cotton are both cellulose fibers. Which statement is true only of rayon?
choices: It absorbs water
It is much weaker when wet than when dry
It comes from a plant
It can be dyed
review.why: Rayon is regenerated cellulose that loses much of its strength when wet, so it needs gentle washing.

review.q: Why do knits need a stretch stitch such as a zigzag?
choices: Knits fray at the edges
Knits are thicker than wovens
Knits stretch, and a straight stitch would pop
Knits are always made of polyester
review.why: Knit loops open when pulled; the seam thread must stretch with them or it breaks.

review.q: Denim and chinos have a diagonal line on the surface. Which weave is that?
choices: Plain
Satin
Jersey
Twill
review.why: Twill's stepped over-under pattern makes a diagonal, and it packs yarns tight for a tough fabric.

review.q: A care tag shows a square with a circle inside and one dot. What is the instruction?
choices: Wash cold
Tumble dry low
Iron on low
Dry clean
review.why: The square is drying, the circle inside it means tumble dry, and one dot means low heat.

review.q: A loose cotton sleeve catches on a gas burner. Based on the burn-test description, what happens?
choices: It goes out on its own once away from the flame
It melts into a bead
It shrinks away from the flame and does not burn
It keeps burning with a yellow flame after it leaves the burner
review.why: Cellulose fibers like cotton catch fast and keep burning after the flame source is removed, which is why sleeves stay rolled near a stove.

review.q: Which fiber choice best fits a fitted athletic shirt for hot weather?
choices: Polyester wicking knit with a little spandex
100% linen plain weave
Wool flannel
Rayon satin
review.why: A wicking polyester knit dries fast, stretches and moves sweat off the skin; the others are too absorbent, too warm or too fragile.
